vignette:
She is a 78-year-old European woman who has spent most of her life in the courtroom, speaking for people who cannot speak for themselves. Even now, when she describes her work as a public defender, her voice carries the same steadiness her colleagues have always relied on. She is married, and her husband has become one of the few people with whom she feels fully unguarded. Before the assault, she had the habits of someone who has long managed pressure well: she kept a full calendar, moved briskly through her days, and prided herself on being prepared for whatever came her way.

The assault happens later in life than she ever expects anything truly dangerous to happen to her. She is leaving a routine errand in daylight, preoccupied with a case and the stack of files in her bag, when a stranger grabs her. It is quick, disorienting, and intimate in the worst way, the kind of attack that strips away her sense of competence before she can marshal it. She remembers the force of being pulled off balance, the shock of realizing she cannot reason her way out of it, and the cold, humiliating panic of having her body controlled by someone else. In the aftermath, she is not only frightened; she is furious with herself for being surprised, as though her lifelong vigilance should have been enough to prevent it.

For the first days afterward, she moves through her home in a kind of stunned practicality. She cleans the clothes she was wearing, answers calls in a clipped voice, and tells her husband she is "fine" with the same tone she has used throughout her career to keep cases moving. But sleep becomes difficult almost immediately. She lies awake listening to the house settle, her mind replaying the assault in pieces she cannot put together or put away. When she does doze, she wakes abruptly, heart racing, sure for a moment that someone is in the room. The smallest unexpected sound makes her jolt. She begins checking locks more than once, and she insists on walking with her husband even for short errands, though she tells herself she simply prefers company.

Returning to work is its own trial. In court, she can still think clearly and argue effectively, but the effort costs her more than it used to. She notices how often she scans exits, how she tenses when someone approaches too quickly in a hallway, how she has begun choosing seats with a wall behind her. She is embarrassed by the change because she has spent decades being the person others look to for composure. She tells herself she is reacting normally, then worries that "normal" should not feel this relentless. There are moments when a client's sudden movement or a raised male voice makes her go cold, and she finds herself answering in a flatter, more controlled tone until she can steady herself. After difficult hearings, she returns home drained and irritable, with less patience than she used to have for minor disruptions.

Her memories of the assault are not constant in a cinematic way; they arrive in fragments, without warning. A hand on her arm from behind in a crowded place can flood her with the same helplessness she felt that day. She avoids certain routes and times of day, especially if she would be alone. She does not tell many people the details, partly because she dislikes being seen as fragile and partly because she does not want to feel the event more fully by speaking it aloud. Yet silence does not spare her. She notices that she is less interested in long social lunches, less inclined to linger in public spaces. Even at home, where she is objectively safe, she has trouble fully relaxing. She startles easily and finds herself listening for what could go wrong next.

What troubles her most is the way the assault has altered her sense of herself. She remains proud, competent, and deeply committed to her work, but she also feels a private drop in confidence that is hard to name. She is aware, with some resentment, that her body reacts before her mind can reassure it. On good days, she can say the event is over and believe it for a while. On harder days, she feels old in a new way, not simply because of her age, but because the attack has made the world feel less predictable and her own body less trustworthy. She continues to show up, to prepare cases, to advocate with precision, but she does so while carrying a quiet, persistent alarm that never seems entirely to switch off.
